name: Carlos Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a kitchen cabinet factory on the old mill road. I run the big panel saw and the edge-bander, the machine that glues the strip along the edge of each board. Every kitchen we make starts on my saw: I load the cutting list, the saw slices up the sheets, and I make sure nothing's out by more than half a millimetre, because if my cut's wrong, the whole kitchen's wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's real. At the end of the week there's a stack of kitchens on the loading dock, and one of them might go in a house down my street. What wears me out is the dust, my back, and the pay, which is lower than it should be for the years I've put in. Rosa works mornings in the school canteen, and between us we get by, but there's nothing left over. Sunday is church and my mother's for lunch, that's what keeps me going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, I told you so. People were acting like the computers were coming for everybody. At church I'd probably say something like, the Lord gave us hands for a reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. I don't use any of that AI stuff, I don't even like the self-checkout. If it stays a fad, I keep my saw and my job, and that's all I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going like now. Keep my head down, do good work, ask the boss again about a raise in the spring. Maybe take a few weekend jobs fitting kitchens for people from church, which I do sometimes for cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a weight I didn't know I was carrying came off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned weekend fitting jobs. How often do those come up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe once a month. Last month I fitted a kitchen for old Mrs Alvarez, a widow from church. Mrs Alvarez paid me in cash and a whole tray of empanadas. That money paid for Mateo's new football boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what money worry stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van. It's got two hundred thousand on the clock. If it dies, I can't do the weekend jobs, and I can't get to work easily either. We'd have to borrow from my brother, and I don't like owing family.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, since people acted like computers were coming for everybody. At church I'd say the Lord gave us hands for a reason.
S0.think: I think I'd be relieved, because I don't use AI and don't even like self-checkouts. If it stays a fad, I keep my saw and my job, which is all I want.
S0.do: Keeps working the panel saw, asks again about a raise in the spring, and keeps taking occasional cash weekend jobs fitting kitchens for people from church.
S0.feel: Calm, like a hidden weight lifted.
S0.quote: Mrs Alvarez paid me in cash and a whole tray of empanadas. That money paid for Mateo's new football boots.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos's world is the saw, the church and his family, and he wants all three to stay as they are. His weekend fitting jobs for neighbours are small but real income. He dislikes owing family, which will matter in harder scenarios.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, if a machine helps, fine, but a kitchen still needs a man who knows wood. The company has the right to buy what it wants, it's their money. But I'd say they'd be foolish to lose their experienced people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the panel saw is already half computer. The next step is a robot that loads the boards, and maybe one that does the edges. I think they'd keep me to watch it, but I'd be babysitting instead of cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big. I'd keep doing my job and wait to see what they actually bring in. If they bring in a new machine, I'd learn the buttons I need, but I'm not going to sit at a computer at night learning AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a strange car parked on your street for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they'd be foolish to lose experienced people. Do you think they'd do it anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, yes, if it saved money. I've seen it. When they brought in the new edge-bander six years ago, they let two older men go the same month. Nobody said it was because of the machine, but we all knew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young Danny on the sanding line. Twenty-two, just had a baby, no qualifications. Sanding is exactly what a robot does well. I'd tell him to get his electrician's ticket while he's young.

S1.say: I'd say a machine is fine if it helps, but a kitchen still needs someone who knows wood. The company has the right to buy what it wants, but losing experienced people would be foolish.
S1.think: I think the saw is already half computer, and robots for loading and edging come next. They'd keep me to watch it, but I'd be babysitting instead of cutting.
S1.do: Keeps doing his job and waits to see what the factory brings in. Learns only the buttons he needs on any new machine and refuses to study AI at night.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a strange car parked on the street for a week.
S1.quote: I think they'd keep me to watch it, but I'd be babysitting instead of cutting.
S1.fieldNote: Carlos defends the company's right to automate while expecting it to drop older workers, as it did six years ago. That tension between free-market belief and lived experience runs through him. He'd learn the minimum on any new machine and nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when a handful of rich tech people decide for everybody. I'd say we should look after our own: family, church, neighbours. I don't want a handout, I want work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished. Two years, the factory has robots doing the cutting and the edges and the fitting, and a man with my diploma and a sore back has nothing to offer. I've got no savings to speak of. I don't know what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything right away: no eating out, sell Rosa's little car, cancel the satellite TV. I'd take any weekend carpentry I could, repairs, fences, anything with my hands while people still pay a person. And I'd swallow my pride and ask my brother and the church for help if the mortgage got close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I'm drowning. Like the ground's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want a handout. Would you take government help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it. My father never took a penny he didn't earn. But if it was that or losing the house with the kids in it, I'd take it, and I'd feel ashamed every time I went to collect it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mateo and Lucia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them God has a plan and we'll get through it as a family. Mateo's fourteen, he'd see through me. Lucia's ten, she'd just hug me. I'd go to the garage afterwards and sit there for an hour.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when a few rich tech people decide for everybody, and we should look after our own through family, church and neighbours. I want work, not a handout.
S2.think: I think I'd be finished, with robots doing cutting, edging and fitting in two years. With my diploma, a sore back and no savings, I don't know what I'd do.
S2.do: Cuts eating out and satellite TV and sells his partner's car straight away. Takes any weekend carpentry or repair work he can find, and asks his brother and the church for help if the mortgage is at risk.
S2.feel: Like he's drowning and the ground has gone.
S2.quote: I'd go to the garage afterwards and sit there for an hour.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario overwhelms Carlos completely. He blames a small group of tech people and leans on family and church, not the state. He'd take government help only to save the house, and with real shame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning and a man should listen to warnings. I'd tell younger guys at work to learn a trade that needs hands in people's homes. And I'd say the company owes its loyal workers some notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast for me. I'd be forty-eight, with my back the way it is. I'd hope they keep me on till the end, but I'd be planning for the day they don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first few years I'd try to save, even just a little, and build up my weekend carpentry so there's something to fall back on. I'd fix up the van so it lasts. Then, honestly, I'd wait and see, because I don't know what else to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but slower. Like a pain that keeps coming back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd build up weekend carpentry. Won't robots do that too, eventually?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I think people will still want a person they know in their kitchen for a while. Mrs Alvarez isn't going to let a robot in her house. That buys me some years, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of time to save and build up the side work. With two years I'm just falling. With five, I can at least put a mattress down before I land.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a warning worth heeding, and tell younger workers to learn a trade that needs hands in people's homes. The company owes loyal workers notice.
S3.think: I think it's still fast for me at forty-eight with a bad back. I'd hope to be kept to the end but plan for the day I'm not.
S3.do: Saves what he can and builds up his weekend carpentry over the first few years. Keeps the van running and waits to see what happens beyond that.
S3.feel: Alarmed but slower, like a pain that keeps coming back.
S3.quote: With five, I can at least put a mattress down before I land.
S3.fieldNote: Carlos's plan for five years is modest: save a little and grow the side carpentry that depends on people trusting a familiar face. He's honest that beyond that he'd wait, because he doesn't know what else to do. Trust and community are his real safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for families to prepare, and families should prepare, not wait for the government. I'd tell young people to get an apprenticeship, a real trade. I'd say it at church and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three. Still need to work, but maybe the mortgage is nearly done. I think I'd get by on side work and whatever's left at the factory, but I'm not going to pretend I'm happy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the years I'd push Mateo into an apprenticeship, electrician or plumber, with someone from church. I'd try to pay off the van and save a little each month. And I'd keep building up the weekend work, maybe start taking on a helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can sleep. It's far enough away to work for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an apprenticeship for Mateo, and not college?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I trust work you can do with your hands. College is a lot of debt for something a computer might do. An apprenticeship pays while you learn, and a man who can fix your heating in winter will always have work, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take on a helper. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Danny from the sanding line, if he's out of work by then. Teach him what I know. The older ones teaching the young ones, not a computer, that's how it should be.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for families to prepare, and they should, not wait for the government. I'd urge young people to get a real trade apprenticeship.
S4.think: I think at fifty-three I'd still need to work, though the mortgage may be nearly done. I'd get by on side work and what's left at the factory, but I wouldn't be happy.
S4.do: Pushes his son into an electrician or plumbing apprenticeship through church contacts. Pays off the van, saves a little each month and grows his weekend carpentry, possibly taking on a younger helper.
S4.feel: Anxious but able to sleep; it's far enough away to work toward.
S4.quote: The older ones teaching the young ones, not a computer, that's how it should be.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Carlos turns toward his son and toward passing on skills. He prefers an apprenticeship to college debt and hopes hand trades will last. His instinct to take on Danny shows his belief in community and work over support from the state.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no doubt. There's no time to do anything. What would help is if companies had to keep their experienced people on for a while and give proper notice, and help with apprenticeships for the young ones. I'd rather have work than a cheque.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Whatever happens, I'll still have my church and my family. That's not nothing. A robot can't take that.

headlineQuote: If my cut's wrong, the whole kitchen's wrong.
portrait: Carlos Torres is a 43-year-old panel saw and edge-bander operator at a kitchen cabinet factory, who never uses AI tools and doesn't even like self-checkouts. Church, family and occasional weekend kitchen-fitting jobs for neighbours anchor his life, and money is tight with almost nothing saved. He's calm about the AI Plateau and only uneasy about Steady Disruption, but AGI in 2 years leaves him panicked, leaning on family and church and taking state help only with shame. With 5 or 10 years his plan stays modest: save a little, grow his side carpentry and push his son into an apprenticeship. He blames a few rich tech people and wants companies to keep loyal workers.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to do anything.
whatWouldHelp: Rules that make companies keep experienced workers for a while and give proper notice, plus help with apprenticeships for young people.
